positions/sanctification-in-the-womb/one: Mary was conceived in the ordinary human condition but was sanctified by God — in the womb (Aquinas) or by her lifelong cooperation with grace and at the Annunciation (Orthodox) — becoming all-holy.
positions/sanctification-in-the-womb/cor: Only Christ was conceived without sin; Mary needed redemption like all descendants of Adam.
God sanctified Mary before birth (as Jeremiah and John the Baptist were set apart) or progressively.
(Orthodox) Mary is Panagia (all-holy), purified by the Holy Spirit at the Annunciation; ancestral sin is understood as inherited mortality, not guilt, so the Western problem does not arise.
Mary's holiness is a victory of grace and freedom, not an exemption from the human condition.
positions/sanctification-in-the-womb/ori: Bernard of Clairvaux's letter to the canons of Lyon (c. 1140) against the new feast; Thomas Aquinas (ST III q. 27); Dominican tradition until 1854. Orthodox theologians (e.g. Gregory Palamas, Nicholas Cabasilas) taught Mary's exceptional holiness; modern Orthodox (Lossky, Bulgakov's critics, Ware) generally reject the 1854 dogma.
positions/sanctification-in-the-womb/str: It preserves the universality of sin and redemption.
It was the view of the greatest medieval doctors of the Church.
Catholic: preservative redemption answers the objection more perfectly.
Protestant: it still affirms Mary's sinlessness beyond Scripture's evidence.
positions/sanctification-in-the-womb/res: Orthodox writers argue that Mary's holiness is more admirable precisely because she shared our fallen condition.
positions/sanctification-in-the-womb/con: Defines a key difference between Catholic and Orthodox Mariology after 1854.
Its Catholic form was set aside by the 1854 definition.
positions/bodily-assumption/oneLine: Having completed the course of her earthly life, Mary was taken up body and soul into heavenly glory, anticipating the resurrection of all believers.
positions/bodily-assumption/coreClaims/0: Mary's body, which bore the Son of God, did not see corruption.
positions/bodily-assumption/coreClaims/1: Her assumption is a consequence of her divine motherhood and sinlessness.
positions/bodily-assumption/coreClaims/2: She anticipates the destiny of the Church (1 Corinthians 15:23).
positions/bodily-assumption/coreClaims/3: Defined ex cathedra by Pius XII (1 November 1950); whether she died first is left open.
positions/bodily-assumption/origin: Transitus Mariae / Dormition narratives from the late 5th century (Syriac, Greek, Coptic, Ethiopic), feast spread in the 6th–7th centuries; Gregory of Tours, John of Damascus; defined by Pius XII in Munificentissimus Deus (1950) after a worldwide consultation of bishops (1946).
positions/bodily-assumption/strongestArg: Ancient and widespread liturgical tradition (East and West) of Mary's end.
No relics of Mary's body were ever claimed, unusual for so venerated a figure.
Fittingness: the ark of the new covenant should not see corruption (Psalm 132:8).
positions/bodily-assumption/strongestObj: No mention in Scripture or in the first four centuries; the narratives are apocryphal.
Protestants and Anglicans question the authority to define it as necessary for faith.
Orthodox share the belief but reject its definition as a dogma by a pope.
positions/bodily-assumption/responses/0: Catholics argue that the living tradition of the Church, not explicit early texts, is the basis; the Church's universal belief in 1950 demonstrated it.
positions/bodily-assumption/responses/1: ARCIC (2005) found the teaching of Mary's glorification consonant with Scripture, though the dogma's authority remained a question.
positions/bodily-assumption/consequences: Feast of 15 August as a major holiday in many countries.
The only ex cathedra papal definition since 1870; ecumenically controversial (C. G. Jung, by contrast, hailed it as a psychological milestone).
positions/dormition/name: Dormition of the Theotokos (Orthodox and Oriental)
positions/dormition/oneLine: Mary truly died (‘fell asleep’) surrounded by the apostles, and was then raised and translated body and soul into heaven — a belief held in the liturgy rather than as a defined dogma.
positions/dormition/coreClaims/0: Mary's death was real, like her Son's.
positions/dormition/coreClaims/1: Christ received her soul and, after burial, her body was taken into heaven.
positions/dormition/coreClaims/2: The belief is expressed in liturgy and icons rather than conciliar definition.
positions/dormition/coreClaims/3: Mary intercedes for the world from heaven.
positions/dormition/origin: Transitus narratives (late 5th century); the feast on 15 August fixed by Emperor Maurice (c. 600); preached by Andrew of Crete, Germanus of Constantinople and John of Damascus (8th century). Coptic and Ethiopian churches celebrate the Assumption on 16 Mesori / Nehasie, after a two-week fast (Filseta).
positions/dormition/strongestArguments/0: It reflects the ancient, shared liturgical memory of East and West.
positions/dormition/strongestArguments/1: It keeps Mary's solidarity with human mortality while honouring her glorification.
positions/dormition/strongestArguments/2: It avoids turning a liturgical mystery into a juridical dogma.
positions/dormition/strongestObjections/: Protestants: it rests on apocryphal narratives without scriptural or early historical basis.
Catholics: if believed universally, it can and should be defined.
positions/dormition/responses/0: Orthodox writers stress that not all truths of the faith need dogmatic definition; the liturgy is itself authoritative.
positions/dormition/consequences/0: A major feast and fast in Orthodox and Oriental churches (Filseta in Ethiopia and Eritrea, Navasard Assumption in Armenia).
positions/dormition/consequences/1: Dormition icons and churches across the Christian East.
positions/intercession-of-saints/name: Intercession and invocation of the saints
positions/intercession-of-saints/altName: Communion of saints (in the Catholic and Orthodox sense)
positions/intercession-of-saints/oneLine: The saints in heaven are alive in Christ and pray for the Church on earth; it is good to ask their prayers and honour them (dulia), and Mary above all (hyperdulia) — worship (latria) belongs to God alone.
positions/intercession-of-saints/coreCla: Death does not sever the communion of the one Body of Christ (Romans 8:38–39).
The prayers of the righteous are powerful (James 5:16), and the saints in heaven pray (Revelation 5:8; 6:9–10).
Asking a saint to pray is like asking a fellow Christian to pray; it does not compete with Christ's mediation.
Relics and shrines are honoured because God worked through the saints' bodies (2 Kings 13:21; Acts 19:12).
positions/intercession-of-saints/origin: Commemoration of martyrs from the 2nd century (Martyrdom of Polycarp, c. 155); inscriptions asking martyrs' prayers in the Roman catacombs (3rd century); the Sub tuum praesidium prayer to the Theotokos; widespread practice by the 4th century; reaffirmed at Nicaea II (787) and Trent, Session XXV (1563).
positions/intercession-of-saints/stronge: It reflects the practice of the early church from at least the 3rd century across East and West.
God is ‘not the God of the dead, but of the living’ (Luke 20:38).
Revelation depicts heavenly beings offering the prayers of the saints.
It expresses the unity of the Church across death.
There is no biblical command or example of praying to departed saints.
Christ is the one mediator (1 Timothy 2:5) and believers have direct access to the Father (Hebrews 4:16).
Saints in heaven cannot hear many prayers at once without omniscience.
In popular practice it has slid into superstition, commerce in relics and effective worship (acknowledged by Trent).
positions/intercession-of-saints/respons: Catholics and Orthodox answer that the saints' knowledge is given by God in the beatific vision, not their own omniscience.
Asking intercession of a living Christian does not violate Christ's mediation; neither does asking a saint.
Abuses are condemned by the church but do not abolish legitimate use.
positions/intercession-of-saints/consequ: Pilgrimage, shrines and patron saints shaped Christian geography and culture (Santiago, Canterbury, Lalibela, Velankanni).
A central target of Reformation critique and iconoclasm.
Local saints became a key means of inculturation in Africa, Asia and the Americas.
positions/sole-mediation-protestant/name: Protestant critique: Christ the sole mediator
positions/sole-mediation-protestant/oneL: Mary is to be honoured as the blessed mother of the Lord and a model of faith, and the saints as examples, but prayers must be addressed to God through Christ alone; invocation of saints and Marian dogmas lack biblical warrant and obscure Christ's sole mediation.
positions/sole-mediation-protestant/core: Christ alone is mediator and intercessor (1 Timothy 2:5; Hebrews 7:25; 1 John 2:1).
Scripture gives no command or example of invoking the departed.
Mary is ‘blessed among women’ and the first believer, a model of grace received — not a source of grace.
The communion of saints is real, but expressed by thanksgiving and imitation, not invocation (Augsburg Confession 21).
Marian dogmas defined since 1854 are not binding because they lack scriptural basis.
positions/sole-mediation-protestant/orig: Late medieval critiques (Wycliffe, Erasmus' satire); Luther (Smalcald Articles 2.2, 1537), Augsburg Confession article 21 (1530), Zwingli, Calvin (Institutes 3.20.21–27), the Thirty-Nine Articles 22 (‘Invocation of Saints… a fond thing vainly invented’).
positions/sole-mediation-protestant/prop: Karl Barth (critic of ‘Mariology’ as the heresy of Catholicism)
positions/sole-mediation-protestant/stro: It rests on explicit biblical teaching about Christ's unique mediation.
It corrects real medieval abuses (sale of relics, indulgences tied to shrines).
Jesus redirected praise of his mother to those who hear the word of God and keep it (Luke 11:27–28).
Prayer to God through Christ is always available and sufficient.
It neglects the early and universal practice of the church.
Asking for prayer from fellow believers is biblical; death does not end the communion of saints.
Protestant reaction has often led to neglect of Mary, contrary to Luke 1:48.
positions/sole-mediation-protestant/resp: Protestants answer that early practice is not self-validating if it lacks apostolic warrant.
Recent Protestant writers (e.g. some Lutherans and Anglicans) have sought to recover honour for Mary without invocation.
positions/sole-mediation-protestant/cons: Removal of shrines, relics and saint-days in Protestant lands; Marian piety largely displaced by Christ-centred and biblical devotion.
Lutherans and Anglicans retained Marian feasts and some images; the Reformed removed images entirely.
Ecumenical dialogue (1990, 2005) seeks common ground on Mary as model and the communion of saints.
positions/icon-veneration/name: Veneration of icons (Second Council of Nicaea)
positions/icon-veneration/oneLine: Because the invisible God became visible in Christ, he and his saints may be depicted; icons receive honourable veneration (proskynesis), which passes to the person depicted, while worship (latreia) is given to God alone.
positions/icon-veneration/coreClaims/0: The incarnation makes God depictable: to refuse images of Christ implies denying his real humanity.
positions/icon-veneration/coreClaims/1: The honour given to an image passes to its prototype (Basil).
positions/icon-veneration/coreClaims/2: Veneration (bowing, kissing, lamps, incense) differs from worship due to God alone.
positions/icon-veneration/coreClaims/3: Icons are ‘Scripture for the illiterate’ and windows of presence in the liturgy.
positions/icon-veneration/coreClaims/4: God himself commanded images (cherubim on the ark, Exodus 25:18–22; the bronze serpent, Numbers 21:8).
positions/icon-veneration/origin: Early Christian art in catacombs and the Dura-Europos house church (c. 240); icons in Byzantine devotion from the 6th century; theology developed by John of Damascus (c. 730) and Theodore the Studite; defined at Nicaea II (787); finally restored in 843 (Triumph of Orthodoxy).
positions/icon-veneration/strongestArgum: Its incarnational logic: if the Word became flesh, the flesh can be portrayed.
Scripture distinguishes idols (false gods) from God-commanded images.
Honour to images parallels honour to the Gospel book, the cross and the emperor's image, accepted by all.
Long-standing use across East, West, Ethiopia, Armenia and Coptic Egypt.
positions/icon-veneration/strongestObjec: The second commandment forbids making images for worship; outward bowing is hard to distinguish from worship in practice.
The divine nature cannot be depicted; an icon of Christ either divides his natures or confuses them (Constantine V).
Popular piety attributed miracles and powers to images themselves.
Some early writers (Epiphanius, Eusebius' letter to Constantia) opposed images of Christ.
positions/icon-veneration/responses/0: Iconodules answer that an icon depicts the person (hypostasis) of Christ, not his divine nature.
positions/icon-veneration/responses/1: They insist veneration is relative and directed to the prototype, while condemning superstition.
positions/icon-veneration/responses/2: The commandment forbids idols of false gods, not all religious images, since God commanded the cherubim.
positions/icon-veneration/consequences/0: Icons became central to Orthodox worship, spirituality and identity, including in Russia, Georgia, the Balkans and Ethiopia.
positions/icon-veneration/consequences/1: The Sunday of Orthodoxy (first Sunday of Lent) annually commemorates 843.
positions/icon-veneration/consequences/2: Western reception was qualified (Libri Carolini, Council of Frankfurt 794), but Catholic image veneration was reaffirmed at Trent.
